newsitem.title: UK: Drugs little good for sore throat, sinuses-studies.
newsitem.headline: Drugs little good for sore throat, sinuses-studies.

text.p: People with sore throats or bad sinus infections may ask for antibiotics, and doctors may be keen to do something to help, but such drugs probably do little good, two studies published on Friday found.
Dr Paul Little and colleagues at Southampton University in England followed up more than 700 people aged four and over who showed up at doctor's surgeries with sore throats.
Most had tonsillitis or pharyngitis, but it did not seem to make much difference if they were given drugs, Little wrote in the British Medical Journal.
Between 30 and 37 percent of patients got better in three days whether they got drugs right away or not at all, and everyone generally recovered after four or five days.
"Prescribing antibiotics for sore throats does not reduce the extent and duration of symptoms," they wrote.
"Patients prescribed antibiotics initially were more likely to think antibiotics were effective and to intend coming back in the future."

There can be some harm in prescribing antibiotics needlessly -- there are theories this has contributed to the rise of antibiotic-resistant bacteria and could weaken peoples' immune systems in general.
"Antibiotics may increase recurrence by altering pharyngeal flora (naturally present and beneficial microbes) and limiting development of immunity," Little's group said.

"Therefore, unless patients with sore throats are very ill, doctors should consider exploring patients' concerns and avoid prescribing antibiotics -- or offer antibiotics if symptoms persist for a few days."

In a separate report in the Lancet medical journal, doctors at St Elisabeth Hospital in Tilburg, Netherlands said giving antibiotics to people with badly inflamed sinuses did not seem to do much good either.
They examined the cases of more than 200 patients with bad sinus infections, as confirmed by x-rays. They were given either amoxycillin or sugar pills.
"Amoxycillin did not influence the clinical course of maxillary sinusitis, nor the frequency of relapses during the one-year follow-up," they wrote.
"Whether antibiotics are necessary in more severe cases warrants further study."
